title: Scenario 1 — Small Commercial Extension
subtitle: Two-storey steel-frame extension with pad foundations, scaffold, MEWP access and a live public interface.

brief.client: Harborne Business Park Ltd (commercial landlord, occupied premises next door)
brief.location: Edge-of-town business park, adjacent to an occupied office building, public footpath and access road
description: You are the Site Manager for a two-storey commercial extension to an occupied office building.
The works include pad foundations, a structural steel frame, metal decking, external envelope, scaffold access, MEWP use and regular deliveries through a shared access road.
The neighbouring building remains occupied throughout, and a public footpath runs along the site frontage.
You must plan the construction phase, set up the site, control high-risk activities and hand the project over safely.
constraints: Occupied office building immediately adjacent to the work area
Public footpath along the site frontage
Shared access road used by the client's visitors and staff
Client wants minimum disruption to their tenants
keyRisks: Work at height (steel erection, scaffold, MEWPs)
Lifting operations near the public and the occupied building
Delivery vehicles sharing access with pedestrians
Temporary instability of the steel frame during erection
Public interface at the site boundary

cppProjectDescription: Two-storey steel-frame commercial extension to an occupied office building, including pad foundations, structural steel, metal decking, envelope and fit-out. Duration 22 weeks. Live public footpath and shared access road on the frontage; adjacent building occupied throughout.

phases.title: Project Brief
phases.intro: Review the project brief and understand what you are being asked to deliver before any planning decisions are made.

steps.title: Your project
body: You have been appointed Site Manager for the principal contractor on a 22-week, £1.4m two-storey extension.
The building next door stays occupied. A public footpath runs along the frontage and deliveries share the client's access road.
Every decision you make will affect safety, legal compliance, programme, cost, quality, the environment, client confidence, workforce morale, enforcement risk and the likelihood of an accident.
keyPoints: Read the constraints — the public interface drives much of your planning
Programme pressure never justifies unsafe decisions
If you don't have enough information, your first duty is to get it

steps.prompt: You receive the contract award letter, but the pre-construction information (PCI) pack from the client team has not yet arrived. What is your first move?
steps.context: Mobilisation is due in three weeks and the commercial team want you to 'get going'.

options.text: Request the pre-construction information immediately and review it before developing the construction phase plan.
options.feedback: Correct. The client must provide pre-construction information, and the principal contractor needs it to plan the construction phase properly. Chasing it early protects both safety and programme.

options.text: Start drafting the plan and logistics from the tender drawings and site visit notes, then reconcile it with the PCI pack when it arrives.
options.feedback: You can begin some logistics thinking, but planning without the PCI risks missing known hazards such as buried services, asbestos surveys or site restrictions.

options.text: Treat the tender pack as the pre-construction information: a two-storey extension on a business park holds few surprises the drawings miss.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Tender drawings are not the PCI. The client must provide proportionate pre-construction information on every project — surveys, services records and site restrictions included.
options.consequence: The tender pack left out the client's asbestos survey and access-road restrictions; the link-corridor break-through had to be re-sequenced at short notice and lost a week.

options.text: Mobilise the groundworks gang on the agreed date to protect the programme, and fold the PCI into the plan once the client's team releases it.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Mobilising without the project's known hazard information means your team starts work blind. This is how buried services get struck and asbestos gets disturbed.
options.criticalFailure: Mobilised without reviewing pre-construction information
options.consequence: Groundworks broke ground before the PCI arrived and the excavator struck a live LV cable shown on the client's utility survey. It was reported to HSE as a dangerous occurrence.

steps.learningNote: Under CDM 2015 the client must provide pre-construction information as soon as practicable. The principal contractor cannot plan the construction phase properly without it, and the construction phase must not start until a suitable construction phase plan is in place.

phases.title: Pre-Construction Planning
phases.intro: Identify the CDM duty holders and confirm competence before anyone sets foot on site.

steps.prompt: The client asks you to confirm who holds which CDM 2015 duties on this project. Which allocation is correct?
steps.context: There is more than one contractor on site, a design team is engaged, and the project will last 22 weeks with around 25 people at peak.

options.text: Client appoints a principal designer and a principal contractor in writing; the project is notifiable so an F10 is submitted; designers and contractors hold their own duties.
options.feedback: Correct. With more than one contractor, the client must appoint a principal designer and principal contractor in writing. Over 30 working days with 20+ workers simultaneously (or 500 person-days) makes the project notifiable to HSE via F10.

options.text: Under the design-and-build contract the principal contractor takes on the client's CDM duties, so we handle the F10, welfare and PCI on its behalf.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Client duties cannot be transferred by contract. Each duty holder retains their own legal responsibilities.
options.consequence: The client believed its duties had passed to you and never checked the time and resources allowed; an HSE visit after the F10 found its arrangements deficient and gave formal advice.

options.text: Formal written PD and PC appointments aren't required on a £1.4m job; the main contractor leads by default and the F10 covers notification.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Appointments depend on there being more than one contractor, not on project value — and if the client fails to appoint, it carries the PD and PC duties itself.
options.consequence: With no principal designer appointed, design risk on the steel connections was never coordinated; the erector found unbuildable details on site and the frame stalled for redesign.

options.text: Let the groundworks start under the enabling-works letter of intent, and finalise the PD and PC appointments once the frame contract is signed.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Without a principal contractor formally appointed, no one legally controls the construction phase — coordination fails exactly when the highest-risk early works happen.
options.criticalFailure: Construction started without CDM duty holders formally appointed
options.consequence: Groundworks ran with no one formally in control; unplanned plant movement collapsed the edge of an unsupported pad excavation beside an operative, and HSE served an improvement notice.

steps.learningNote: Know the six duty holders: client, principal designer, designer, principal contractor, contractor and worker. Appointments must be in writing, and F10 notification applies when work exceeds 30 working days with 20+ workers at once, or 500 person-days.

cppText.best: Client: Harborne Business Park Ltd. Principal Designer and Principal Contractor appointed in writing. Project notified to HSE (F10 displayed on site). All contractors briefed on their CDM duties.
cppText.partial: Duty holder allocation recorded but appointment evidence incomplete.
cppText.poor: Duty holders not clearly identified — legal appointments outstanding.
cppText.unsafe: Duty holders not appointed before works commenced — non-compliant.

steps.prompt: You are appointing the steelwork and scaffold subcontractors. How do you check they are suitable?

options.text: Assess capability and competence for this scope: comparable experience, training and card records, resources for the dates, and the quality of their RAMS.
options.feedback: Correct. CDM requires those appointing contractors to take reasonable steps to ensure skills, knowledge, experience and organisational capability.

options.text: Shortlist on price, then confirm each firm holds current SSIP accreditation and valid CSCS/CISRS cards for the whole gang — that covers the competence check.
options.feedback: Accreditation and cards are a useful starting point, but they are not a competence assessment for this scope — experience, resources and RAMS quality still need checking.
options.consequence: The cheapest scaffold firm had never built a loading bay of this size; its first design submission was rejected by the TW designer and scaffold handover slipped a week.

options.text: Appoint the steel and scaffold firms the client has used on its other buildings on the park — their track record here is the best evidence available.
options.feedback: The duty to check capability sits with the appointer. A client recommendation and past work elsewhere do not discharge it — you still need evidence for this scope.
options.consequence: The client's preferred steel erector had only built single-storey frames; its gang arrived without trained MEWP operators and erection started three days late.

options.text: Rely on each specialist's own pre-qualification: both are established firms, so their RAMS and training records can be reviewed once they mobilise.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Leaving the checks until after mobilisation means unverified 'specialists' are already working — a recurring factor in scaffold and steel erection failures.
options.criticalFailure: High-risk trade contractors appointed without competence checks
options.consequence: The scaffold lead hand held no CISRS card and tied a lift wrongly; a section partially collapsed under load and was reported under RIDDOR as a dangerous occurrence.

steps.topic: Competence — skills, knowledge, experience and organisational capability
steps.learningNote: Competence checks must be proportionate to the risk of the work. For high-risk trades (scaffold, steel, lifting), review trade-specific qualifications, training records, RAMS quality and past performance.

cppText.best: All contractors assessed for skills, knowledge, experience and organisational capability before appointment. Trade-specific competence (scaffolding, steel erection, lifting) verified. Training records held on site; site induction mandatory for all.
cppText.partial: Competence checks partially completed; gaps to close before high-risk works.
cppText.poor: Competence assessment inadequate — appointments made on cost/recommendation only.
cppText.unsafe: No competence verification for high-risk trades — non-compliant.

steps.prompt: Put the pre-construction and mobilisation activities into a safe, legal order — from appointment through to the first high-risk work on site.
steps.context: Two-storey steel-frame extension, 22 weeks, around 25 people at peak and more than one contractor. Pad excavations beside the public footpath are the first high-risk work.

activities.label: Client appoints the PD and PC in writing
activities.detail: Needed because there is more than one contractor; the client cannot pass its own duties on.

activities.label: Obtain and review the pre-construction information
activities.detail: Asbestos survey of the existing wall, utility records, ground investigation, client's site rules.

activities.label: Client submits the F10 notification to HSE
activities.detail: Notifiable: over 30 working days with more than 20 workers at once. A copy is displayed on site.

activities.label: Check competence and appoint key subcontractors
activities.detail: Groundworks, steel and scaffold: experience, resources, card records and RAMS quality.

activities.label: Prepare the CPP for the initial works
activities.detail: Welfare, emergency arrangements, traffic management, site rules and the groundworks risks.

activities.label: Appoint the TWC and open the temporary works register
activities.detail: Hoarding, cabin bases, excavation support and crane platform listed with design check categories.

activities.label: Mobilise: welfare, hoarding, gates and traffic management
activities.detail: The construction phase starts here — welfare is live from the first day.

activities.label: Locate services and start pad excavations under permit
activities.detail: CAT and Genny scan, trial holes, permit to dig, inducted and briefed groundworks gang.

constraints.reason: The principal contractor's duty to prepare the CPP flows from its written appointment — until then nobody is formally responsible for planning the construction phase.
The CPP must be built on the client's pre-construction information; surveys, services records and site restrictions shape the plan.
The F10 names the principal designer and principal contractor, so they must be appointed before it is submitted.
Notification has to reach HSE before the construction phase begins.
The construction phase must not start until a suitable CPP is in place — mobilising first means working beside the public with no emergency, welfare or traffic arrangements.
The hoarding and cabin bases are temporary works in their own right — the TWC and register must exist before they are installed.
The groundworks contractor must be checked and appointed, with its excavation RAMS reviewed, before it starts digging.
Support for 2.4 m pad excavations is temporary works — it must be designed, checked and released by the TWC before anyone digs.
Digging beside a public footpath before the hoarding, gates and welfare are in place exposes the public to open excavations and leaves workers without welfare.
Utility records and ground investigation data in the PCI tell the survey team what to look for before ground is broken.

steps.learningNote: Appointments come first, because duties flow from them. The CPP is built from the pre-construction information and must be in place before the construction phase starts; the F10 goes in before work begins; temporary works control exists before the first temporary works go up. Nothing high-risk starts until site set-up, induction and the relevant permit are in place.

phases.title: Construction Phase Plan
phases.intro: The construction phase plan (CPP) is your project's safety management backbone. Get it right, keep it proportionate, and keep it live.

steps.prompt: The client wants mobilisation brought forward a week. The construction phase plan is drafted but the emergency arrangements, traffic management and first high-risk RAMS are incomplete. Can the construction phase start?

options.text: No. Complete the plan for the initial works first — including welfare, emergency and traffic arrangements — before anyone starts on site.
options.feedback: Correct. The construction phase must not begin until a suitable CPP is in place and welfare is provided. Explain this to the client — a short pause now prevents enforcement and injury later.

options.text: Start with site clearance and hoarding only under a short interim plan, and complete the emergency and traffic sections during the first week.
options.feedback: A phased plan is acceptable only if the plan genuinely covers the works being done — but emergency and welfare arrangements are needed from day one, so they cannot wait.

options.text: Start on the client's date, using the company's generic emergency and traffic procedures as a stop-gap until the site-specific sections are written.
options.feedback: Incorrect. Generic company procedures don't describe this site's footpath crossing, muster point or the neighbour's fire arrangements — the plan must cover the initial works before they begin.
options.consequence: The generic procedure named no muster point; when the neighbouring office's fire alarm sounded, operatives gathered on the shared access road among the client's evacuating staff.

options.text: Start on the client's date and date the CPP as issued at mobilisation; the remaining sections can be written up over the first fortnight.
options.feedback: Never falsify safety documents. Dating an incomplete plan as issued is a serious legal breach that destroys any defence you might have had.
options.criticalFailure: Considered falsifying the construction phase plan
options.consequence: An HSE inspector following up the F10 found the 'issued' CPP had no emergency or traffic sections, served an improvement notice and charged a fee for intervention.

steps.learningNote: The CPP must be in place before the construction phase begins, must be proportionate to the project, and must be reviewed and updated as the project changes. Welfare and emergency arrangements are day-one requirements.

cppText.best: Site rules established before mobilisation: induction mandatory, PPE standards, permit requirements, exclusion zones, no unaccompanied visitors, speed limits, banned substances, housekeeping standards.
cppText.partial: Interim site rules issued; full set to follow in week one.
cppText.unsafe: No site rules in place at start of construction phase.

steps.prompt: Which approach makes the construction phase plan most useful on this project?

options.text: A proportionate plan built around this site's real risks — public interface, steel erection, lifting, work at height — and updated as the job develops.
options.feedback: Correct. A CPP is a working management tool. It should reflect the actual site, name real people, and change when the project changes.

options.text: The company's standard 120-page CPP template with the project name, contacts and programme inserted — it covers every topic an HSE inspector might ask about.
options.feedback: Generic bulk hides the few pages that matter. Inspectors and courts see straight through unedited templates — and so do your supervisors.
options.consequence: Supervisors never found the footpath and delivery rules buried in the template; a driver unloaded on the public footpath and a tenant lodged a formal complaint with the client.

options.text: A short four-page plan covering site rules, contacts, welfare and emergencies — it's a modest extension and supervisors will actually read it.
options.feedback: Brevity helps people read it, but proportionate does not mean minimal. Steel erection, lifting and a live public interface demand a substantive plan.

options.text: Adapt the CPP from your last steel-frame office job — same frame type, same erector, same crane hire — updating the names, dates and site plan.
options.feedback: Every site is different. An adapted plan will miss this project's specific hazards, such as the occupied neighbouring building and the public footpath.
options.consequence: The adapted plan carried over the last site's crane position and said nothing about the occupied office; the lift plan had to be redone and steel erection slipped four days.

steps.learningNote: Ask of every CPP: does it identify this site's hazards, name responsibilities, and set out workable arrangements? If a section wouldn't change how anyone works, question why it's there.

phases.title: Site Set-Up
phases.intro: Lay out the site. Drag items from the palette onto the plan. Think about the public boundary, segregation of vehicles and pedestrians, welfare position, and what belongs away from drains and the public.

steps.prompt: Place the site set-up items on the plan. The public road and footpath run along the top; the occupied office building is to the right; the new extension footprint is in the centre. Place every required item where it is safest and most practical.

rules.placementNote: Solid hoarding along the public boundary separates the public from the works.
Vehicle gate at the designated entrance, with visibility of the footpath crossing.
Separate pedestrian gate so people never enter through the vehicle gate.
Statutory signage and site rules at the entrance where everyone sees them.
Access control at the entrance stops unauthorised entry.
Lighting to entrance and circulation routes.
Segregated pedestrian route from the gate to welfare and the work area.
One-way delivery route to laydown, kept clear of the pedestrian route.
Traffic management (banksman point, barriers, crossing) where vehicles cross the public footpath.
Welfare near the entrance, on the pedestrian route, away from the works.
Toilets and washing adjacent to the welfare cabin.
Site office and induction room near the entrance.
First aid point in/next to welfare, clearly signed.
Fire point on the escape route with alarm, extinguishers and signage.
Muster point in open space, away from the building and the crane zone.
Skips on firm ground on the vehicle route, clear of the public boundary.
Laydown on the delivery route, not blocking access or escape.
Bunded fuel storage well away from drains, boundaries and ignition sources.
Spill kit beside fuel storage and refuelling point.
Protect the surface water drain from silt and spills.
Plant parked on firm level ground, keys controlled.
Scaffold around the extension footprint.
Crane position with radius clear of the public and the occupied building.
Pad foundation excavations within the protected work area.
Exclusion zone under lifting and steel erection operations.
Protection (fan/gantry/barriers) where the scaffold and lifting interface with the footpath.

steps.learningNote: A good site set-up separates the public from the works, separates vehicles from pedestrians, puts welfare where people enter, keeps fuel away from drains, and gives every high-risk activity its own controlled zone.

steps.prompt: Deliveries must cross the public footpath to enter site. What traffic management arrangement do you set?

options.text: Booked delivery slots, a trained marshal controlling the footpath crossing, physical barriers, clear sightlines, public signage and a one-way route inside site.
options.feedback: Correct. The vehicle/pedestrian interface at the boundary is one of this site's highest risks — it needs positive control, not just signs.

options.text: Advance warning signs on both sides of the crossing, a convex mirror at the gate, and hazard lights and audible alarms on every delivery vehicle.
options.feedback: Signs, mirrors and alarms don't control the risk. Members of the public — including children and people with impaired sight or hearing — cannot be relied on to react.

options.text: Brief every delivery driver at booking to crawl across the footpath with hazard lights on and sound the horn, as they know their own vehicle's blind spots best.
options.feedback: Relying on driver vigilance at a public interface is not a control measure — blind spots are exactly what a driver cannot see.
options.consequence: A reversing tipper crossed the footpath with no marshal and stopped within a metre of a pedestrian. A tenant reported the near miss and the client demanded a review.

options.text: Keep the gate clear by letting early deliveries wait on the public road with hazard lights on, and call each one in when the yard is ready.
options.feedback: Queuing on the live road creates a new hazard for road users and the public and will attract enforcement attention.
options.criticalFailure: Uncontrolled vehicle/public interface at site entrance
options.consequence: A waiting artic on the public road pushed pedestrians into the carriageway; a cyclist hit the trailer and was taken to hospital. The police and highway authority investigated.

steps.learningNote: Plan traffic like any other high-risk activity: segregate, control crossings with a marshal, schedule deliveries, and design the route so reversing is eliminated or controlled.

cppText.best: Delivery booking system in place. Trained traffic marshal controls the footpath crossing. Physical segregation of vehicles and pedestrians, one-way internal route, reversing minimised, 5 mph site speed limit, warning signage to the public.
cppText.partial: Signage and mirrors at the entrance; marshal arrangements to be confirmed.
cppText.poor: Traffic management limited to driver instructions — inadequate for the public interface.
cppText.unsafe: No effective traffic management at the public interface.

phases.title: Welfare and Access
phases.intro: Welfare is a day-one legal requirement, and controlled access protects everyone — including the public.

steps.prompt: The welfare units arrive but can't be connected to services until day three. Groundworks want to start on day one. What do you do?

options.text: Provide compliant interim welfare from day one — serviced units or agreed suitable facilities — otherwise no start.
options.feedback: Correct. Toilets, washing with warm water, drinking water, rest facilities and drying space are required from the first day of the construction phase, not from week two.

options.text: Start on day one and arrange for the gang to use the café toilets across the road for the two days until the cabins are connected.
options.feedback: Public facilities you don't control are not compliant welfare provision. This is one of the most common HSE enforcement topics on small sites.
options.consequence: The café withdrew permission on day two; with nowhere to wash after handling wet concrete, a groundworker was treated for cement burns to his hands.

options.text: Start on day one with a hired chemical toilet and bottled drinking water — the cabins' washing and drying rooms will be live by day three.
options.feedback: Inadequate. Washing with warm water, soap and drying, plus rest facilities, are required from day one — a toilet and drinking water alone are not enough.
options.consequence: An HSE inspector on a routine visit found no washing facilities on site, served an improvement notice on welfare provision and charged a fee for intervention.

options.text: Hold all work until day three when the cabins are connected, and accept the two-day slip rather than improvise welfare arrangements.
options.feedback: Safe but unimaginative — compliant interim welfare could have protected both people and programme.

steps.learningNote: Schedule 2 welfare requirements apply from day one: toilets, washing with hot and cold water, drinking water, rest room, changing/drying facilities. Welfare readiness should gate mobilisation in your programme.

cppText.best: Welfare from day one: toilets, washing with warm water, drinking water, heated rest room with means to warm food, drying room, secure changing. Cleaned and maintained daily. Sized for peak workforce of 25.
cppText.partial: Welfare provision delayed/interim — brought to full compliance during week one.
cppText.poor: Welfare provision inadequate at start of works.
cppText.unsafe: No compliant welfare at start of works.

steps.prompt: How do you control who comes onto site?

options.text: Induction before first entry, daily signing in and out, cards checked, visitors escorted, and the public kept out by secure hoarding and locked gates.
options.feedback: Correct. Access control is the foundation of site security and emergency roll-call — you must know who is on site at all times.

options.text: Induct new starters at the first tea break so they aren't stood idle, with the gang's foreman keeping them close by until then.
options.feedback: Induction must come before exposure to site hazards, not after.
options.consequence: A new labourer, not yet inducted, walked under a live steel lift on his first morning. The slinger stopped the lift in time and the near miss was reported.

options.text: Sign-in and induction for all contractors; the landlord's facilities staff keep their own building passes and walk through to the plant room as they need.
options.feedback: The construction site is under your control, not the client's. Client staff on site without induction and escort are unprotected visitors.
options.consequence: A landlord's facilities engineer walked through to the plant room during a steel lift and entered the exclusion zone. The lift was stopped and the client was formally notified.

options.text: Hold the vehicle gate open during working hours so deliveries flow, with the site office window overlooking the entrance for supervision.
options.feedback: An open, unattended gate next to a public footpath invites unauthorised access, including children — a view from a window is not control.
options.criticalFailure: Site left open to unauthorised access
options.consequence: A member of the public walked in through the open gate looking for the office reception and fell into an open pad excavation, breaking his leg. HSE investigated.

steps.learningNote: The principal contractor must take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised access. Induction, signing in/out, escorting visitors and physical security are your core controls — and the signing-in record is your emergency roll-call.

cppText.best: Site induction for all before first entry. Daily briefings, weekly toolbox talks, method statement briefings before each new task, notice board with F10/insurance/site rules, translation support arranged where needed.
cppText.partial: Induction in place; briefing schedule to be formalised.

steps.prompt: Set the emergency and first aid arrangements for the site.

options.text: Assessed first aid cover with named first aiders on every shift, a signed first aid point, a plan for fire, rescue from height and serious injury, and a muster point — all briefed at induction.
options.feedback: Correct. Emergency arrangements must exist before the emergency — including rescue from height and contact with the neighbouring building's fire marshal.

options.text: A stocked first aid kit in the site office, emergency numbers on the induction board, and the 999 service relied on for anything serious.
options.feedback: A first aid box is not first aid provision. You need assessed cover, trained people and a plan for foreseeable emergencies including rescue from height.

options.text: Use the steel erectors' qualified first aider as the site's cover, since they're present for the highest-risk weeks, backed by the office first aid kit.
options.feedback: Cover must exist for everyone on site at all times, not only when one subcontractor is present.
options.consequence: On a day the erectors were off site, a groundworker gashed his forearm on steel banding; no first aider was present and a colleague had to drive him to A&E.

options.text: Finalise the emergency and rescue plan before steel erection starts; groundworks and set-up are low-level work covered by the generic site rules.
options.feedback: Excavation, deliveries and site set-up all carry serious injury potential. Emergency arrangements are a day-one requirement, not a steelwork one.
options.criticalFailure: No emergency arrangements during early works
options.consequence: When a groundworker was struck by a reversing dumper, nobody knew who led the response or how to direct the ambulance in; HSE's investigation criticised the delay.

steps.learningNote: Assess first aid needs against the workforce and the risks. Plan for foreseeable emergencies: fire, collapse, rescue from height and from excavations, serious injury, and coordinate with neighbours who share the interface.

cppText.best: Emergency plan covers fire, serious injury, rescue from height and excavation, structural incident and public interface incidents. Named first aiders each shift; first aid point signed; muster point established; emergency contacts displayed; liaison with neighbouring building's fire warden.
cppText.partial: Basic first aid and 999 arrangements; rescue planning to be completed before work at height.
cppText.unsafe: No emergency arrangements in place during early works.

phases.title: Hazard Identification
phases.intro: Walk the job on paper before it exists. Which hazards deserve your management attention first?

steps.prompt: Walk the site and flag every condition that needs action before work carries on. Leave acceptable conditions unflagged — false alarms waste supervisors' time and cost you credibility with the trades.
steps.location: Site walk-round — Tuesday 07:40. Link-corridor pads still open, first steel bay decked, crane setting up for bay two.

observations.text: Pad excavation 2.4 m deep with vertical, unsupported sides; a loaded dumper is parked a metre from the edge.
observations.explanation: Hazard (temporary works). At 2.4 m, unsupported vertical sides can collapse without warning, and the dumper surcharges the edge. Install the designed support or batter the sides, keep plant back behind stop blocks, and inspect before anyone enters.

observations.text: Traffic marshal holding pedestrians at the footpath barrier while a lorry turns in through the vehicle gate.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. This is the planned control: a trained marshal positively stops the public while the vehicle crosses, backed by physical barriers rather than signs alone.

observations.text: Safety nets rigged under the first-floor leading edge; the net tag shows an inspection this morning.
observations.explanation: Acceptable (temporary works / work at height). Collective fall protection is in place below the working edge and has been inspected, so it protects everyone without relying on individual behaviour.

observations.text: Scaffold loading bay holding three pallets of blocks; the safe working load sign on the bay gate reads two pallets.
observations.explanation: Hazard (temporary works). The bay is designed for its displayed load; exceeding it overloads the bay, its ties and the scaffold below. Offload the excess, brief the telehandler driver and gang, and have the bay inspected before it is loaded again.

observations.text: 110 V cables run on insulated hooks along the hoarding, above head height on the walkway.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. The cables are off the floor and clear of pedestrians and barrows, which removes the trip hazard and protects the cables from damage.

observations.text: Tipper reversing across the footpath crossing while the traffic marshal signs a delivery ticket at the gate.
observations.explanation: Hazard. The marshal is the control for the public interface; while they are distracted, a reversing vehicle with blind spots crosses a live footpath. Stop the vehicle, restore marshalled control, and keep paperwork away from marshalling duties.

observations.text: Operative dry-cutting concrete blocks with a disc cutter, wearing an FFP3 mask over a full beard.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Dry cutting releases respirable crystalline silica, and a tight-fitting mask cannot seal over a beard. Use water suppression or on-tool extraction, and RPE that suits the wearer (such as a powered hood) if the beard stays.

observations.text: Crane outriggers on engineered mats on the compacted platform; the TWC's signed permit to load is in the crane cab.
observations.explanation: Acceptable (temporary works). The platform and mats were designed for the outrigger loads, checked, and released by the TWC's permit to load — the hold point has been passed.

observations.text: Propane cylinders chained upright in a ventilated, locked cage, well away from the cabins and the office.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. The cylinders are upright, secured, ventilated and separated from buildings and combustibles, limiting both fire spread and tampering.

observations.text: First-floor deck edge: a 1.5 m length of barrier lifted out to land a bundle, not yet refitted, no net below.
observations.explanation: Hazard (temporary works / work at height). An open leading edge with no collective protection beneath is a fall of several metres. Refit the barrier now; any planned removal to land loads needs a permit and nets or restraint in place first.

observations.text: Pad excavation 2.4 m deep with a trench box in place, spoil set back, and this shift's inspection signed.
observations.explanation: Acceptable (temporary works). Support is in place, spoil is set back to avoid surcharging the edge, and the excavation has been inspected at the start of the shift as required.

observations.text: 110 V extension lead trailed across the pedestrian walkway outside the welfare cabins.
observations.explanation: Hazard. A trip hazard on the busiest pedestrian route, and the lead is exposed to damage from boots and barrows. Re-route it overhead on cable hooks or use a cable protector, and add cable management to housekeeping checks.

observations.text: Concrete pump outrigger sitting on stacked timber packing over a recently backfilled drainage trench.
observations.explanation: Hazard (temporary works / ground bearing). Backfill and improvised packing have unknown bearing capacity; an outrigger punching through can overturn the pump boom towards the footpath or office. Stop the set-up until the outrigger sits on suitable mats on verified ground.

observations.text: Operative cutting blocks with a water-fed disc cutter, clean-shaven and wearing an FFP3 mask.
observations.explanation: Acceptable. Water suppression controls the silica dust at source, and the FFP3 mask is a backup worn on a clean-shaven face so it can seal.

observations.text: Propane cylinders stood among the cladding insulation stack, against the occupied office's wall.
observations.explanation: Hazard. Gas cylinders beside combustible insulation and an occupied building turn any fire into a serious one. Move the cylinders to a secure, ventilated store away from buildings, and store insulation away from hot works and the office.

observations.text: Scaffold tag at the access ladder shows the handover certificate and an inspection five days ago.
observations.explanation: Acceptable (temporary works). The scaffold has been handed over and inspected within the 7-day statutory interval, and the tag shows users its status at the point of access.

steps.topic: Hazard identification — site inspection and temporary works
steps.learningNote: Look for the control, not the activity. The same excavation, loading bay, crane outrigger or cutting task can be acceptable or dangerous depending on support, load limits, verified bearing and source control. Temporary works hazards are often silent until they fail — judge them against their design and permit, not by eye.

steps.prompt: Which set of hazards should be treated as the priority 'principal risks' for this project?

options.text: Work at height and steel erection, lifting near the public and the office, vehicle/pedestrian interfaces, excavation collapse and buried services, and temporary frame instability.
options.feedback: Correct. These are the credible fatal-injury risks on this project, and each needs specific planning, not generic controls.

options.text: Slips and trips, manual handling and silica dust — industry data shows these cause the largest share of injuries and ill-health on sites like this.
options.feedback: These matter and must be managed, but frequency isn't severity — your planning priority goes to the risks that kill.

options.text: The hazards the steel, scaffold and groundworks subcontractors identify in their own RAMS — they're closest to the work and manage their own interfaces.
options.feedback: The principal contractor must plan, manage and coordinate the whole construction phase, including interfaces no single subcontractor sees.
options.consequence: No one owned the interface between the crane's slew and the scaffold loading bay; a swinging beam struck the scaffold guardrail and the bay was closed for repair.

options.text: COSHH, noise and vibration — the risks with specific regulations and exposure limits that HSE inspectors target on visits to sites like this.
options.feedback: Health risks are important, but this misses the immediate fatal risks that dominate this project — falls, lifting, vehicles and excavations.
options.consequence: Excavation support was never prioritised; a pad excavation side slumped overnight beside the plant route and a dumper driver stopped short of the edge.

steps.learningNote: Prioritise by severity and credibility: falls from height, lifting failures, vehicle strikes, excavation collapse and structural instability are the classic construction killers. Health risks then need parallel, longer-term management.

cppText.best: Principal risks identified: work at height, steel erection, lifting adjacent to public/occupied building, vehicle-pedestrian interface, excavation collapse, buried services, temporary instability of steel frame. Each has specific RAMS, exclusion zones and supervision arrangements. Frequent-injury risks (slips/trips, manual handling, dust, noise) controlled through housekeeping standards, task rotation and health surveillance.
cppText.partial: Main risks identified; interface risks need further coordination.
cppText.poor: Risk identification left to individual subcontractors.
cppText.unsafe: No structured hazard identification for the project.

riskEntry.hazard: Falls from height / steel erection / lifting near public
riskEntry.control: Specific RAMS, exclusion zones, supervision and coordination by PC

steps.prompt: The design shows hot works (welding of steel connections) and combustible envelope materials stored on site. What is your fire prevention approach?

options.text: A site fire plan: hot work permits with fire watch, combustibles stored away from hot work and the office, fire points, alarm, and escape routes agreed with the office.
options.feedback: Correct. Fire on a site attached to an occupied building threatens people you can't see. The fire plan must cover both.

options.text: Fire points with extinguishers at each exit, no-smoking signs across the site, and a fire watch whenever the welders judge one is needed.
options.feedback: Equipment without a plan. Fire safety is about preventing ignition, controlling fuel and ensuring escape — and the fire watch shouldn't be left to the welder's judgement.

options.text: Ban all hot works and require bolted connections and cold-cutting throughout, even where the steel details assume some site welding.
options.feedback: Eliminating hot works where practical is good hierarchy thinking, but a blanket ban you can't sustain breeds unofficial workarounds — worse than a controlled permit system.

options.text: Make each hot-works subcontractor responsible for its own permits, extinguishers and fire watch under its RAMS, with the requirement written into each subcontract order.
options.feedback: Uncoordinated hot works next to an occupied building is a serious fire risk. The PC owns the site fire plan, including how permits interact with storage and the neighbour's escape routes.
options.criticalFailure: No coordinated fire plan next to occupied building
options.consequence: Welding sparks ignited cladding insulation stacked against the office wall. The office was evacuated and the fire service attended; the fire authority and HSE investigated.

steps.learningNote: Think fuel, ignition, escape: control combustible storage, permit every hot work with a fire watch and cool-down period, protect escape routes, and integrate your plan with any attached occupied premises.

cppText.best: Fire plan: hot work permit system with trained fire watch and 60-minute cool-down checks; combustible materials stored away from the building and ignition sources; fire points with alarm at agreed locations; escape routes and muster point signed and maintained; weekly alarm test; liaison with occupied building's fire marshal; waste removed regularly to prevent accumulation.
cppText.partial: Fire points and extinguishers provided; permit system to be implemented before hot works start.
cppText.poor: Fire arrangements left to individual contractors.
cppText.unsafe: No coordinated fire plan for site attached to occupied building.

phases.title: RAMS Review
phases.intro: Risk assessments and method statements only protect people if they are specific, practical, communicated — and actually followed on the ground.

steps.prompt: The scaffold contractor has arrived before the scaffold design information and handover arrangements are confirmed. The client is pushing for work to start today. What should you do?

options.text: Let the gang start the base lifts on the rear elevation, which the supervisor says is a standard configuration, while the loading bay design is finalised this week.
options.feedback: Unsafe. Erecting scaffold before the design information is confirmed has caused collapses onto workers and the public — and the rear lifts tie into the same structure as the loading bay.
options.criticalFailure: Scaffold erection allowed without design and handover controls
options.consequence: The early lifts didn't suit the loading bay design; a section partially collapsed when loaded with boards, was reported under RIDDOR as a dangerous occurrence, and was rebuilt.

options.text: Let erection start today and have the TWC inspect the completed scaffold against the design before it is handed over for use.
options.feedback: Inspection after the event cannot retrofit a missing design or competence check — the risk is taken during erection, before any handover.
options.consequence: The finished scaffold failed the TWC's check against the later design — tie spacing and the loading bay were wrong — and two days were lost to strip and rebuild.

options.text: Hold the start: confirm the design or standard solution, the RAMS, the gang's cards, and the inspection and handover arrangements before work proceeds.
options.feedback: Correct. Work should not proceed until the required information, competence, RAMS, inspection and handover controls are confirmed. Programme pressure must not override safe planning.

options.text: Ask the operatives whether they're happy it's a configuration they've built many times before, and record their confirmation in the site diary.
options.feedback: Workers' views matter, but they cannot substitute for design information and management controls — and they may feel pressured to say yes.
options.consequence: The gang's confidence was misplaced: the loading bay needed a design. The TWC stopped loading after the first pallet and the bay was rebuilt.

steps.topic: Scaffold — design, RAMS and handover control
steps.learningNote: Every scaffold needs either a recognised standard configuration or a bespoke design, erected by competent scaffolders, with a handover certificate before use and statutory inspections thereafter. No information, no erection.

cppText.best: Scaffold: design/standard configuration confirmed before erection; erection by competent scaffolders; handover certificate before first use; tagged; inspected every 7 days and after alteration or adverse weather.
cppText.partial: Scaffold controls partially confirmed at erection stage.
cppText.poor: Scaffold erection started ahead of confirmed controls.
cppText.unsafe: Scaffold erected without design information or handover controls.

steps.prompt: The steel erection method statement arrives. It is 40 pages, mostly generic, and doesn't mention the occupied building, the crane position or the partially-erected frame's stability. Do you accept it?

options.text: Reject it with comments and require a site-specific revision — erection sequence, temporary stability, lift plan interface, the occupied building — before steel starts.
options.feedback: Correct. A method statement that doesn't describe this site cannot brief the workforce or control the risk. Review is a real gate, not a filing exercise.

options.text: Accept it for the record, and email the erector a list of your conditions on sequence, stability and working next to the occupied office.
options.feedback: Conditions in an email rarely reach the operatives doing the work. The controlling document itself must be right.

options.text: Accept it: the erector is BCSA-registered, has built many similar frames, and its insurers accept the method — the site-specific detail is covered by the separate lift plan.
options.feedback: Membership, experience and insurance don't make a generic method site-specific. Insurance pays after people are hurt; RAMS review exists to prevent the event.
options.consequence: With no site-specific sequence, the gang erected the first bay without the bracing the designer expected; the frame racked in a gust and erection stopped until it was braced.

options.text: Rewrite the sequence and stability sections yourself tonight from the drawings, and issue them to the gang so the programme holds.
options.feedback: The contractor must own their method — a method statement written by someone else's site manager won't match how their gang actually works.
options.consequence: Your rewritten sequence didn't match how the gang erects; they fell back on their own method and the TWC halted erection for a day to reconcile the two.

steps.learningNote: Test RAMS against: is it specific to this site and task? Is the sequence workable? Are interfaces covered? Who supervises? How is it briefed? If you can't picture the work from it, reject it.

phases.title: Temporary Works Register
phases.intro: Identify every temporary works item, then set the right level of design, checking, inspection and control for each. Appoint your temporary works coordinator first.

steps.prompt: Who manages temporary works on this project, and how?

options.text: Appoint a trained TWC in writing, keep a TW register, set design check categories per item, and enforce permits to load and strike at hold points.
options.feedback: Correct. A named, competent TWC operating a register with hold points is the recognised way to manage temporary works risk.

options.text: As site manager, keep a temporary works list in the site diary and personally sign off each item before it is loaded or struck.
options.feedback: Without a formally appointed TWC, a maintained register and design check categories, items get loaded before checks — the classic route to collapse.
options.consequence: The diary list missed the crane outrigger mats; nobody verified the platform design before the crane arrived, and the first day of lifting was lost to checks.

options.text: Each specialist manages its own temporary works under its own procedure — the scaffolder, groundworker and steel erector each have a trained TWS.
options.feedback: Temporary works interact — scaffold ties, crane mats and excavations affect each other. Coordination must sit above the individual trades.
options.consequence: Excavation support and scaffold bases were planned separately; a scaffold standard was found bearing on the edge of a pad excavation and the lift had to be struck.

options.text: Use the company's standard scaffold and excavation details throughout, so no separate temporary works procedure is needed on a job of this size and duration.
options.feedback: Standard details are still temporary works needing registration and control — and this project also has crane mats and a steel frame that must be stabilised during erection.
options.criticalFailure: No temporary works management arrangements
options.consequence: With no TW procedure, the part-erected frame was left unbraced overnight; wind pushed two columns out of plumb over the exclusion zone and HSE prohibited further erection.

steps.learningNote: The TWC controls the register, ensures design and checking at the right category, and operates hold points (permit to load / permit to strike). The role must be appointed in writing with defined authority to stop work.

cppText.best: Temporary Works Coordinator appointed in writing. TW register maintained covering scaffold, excavations, crane/MEWP mats, edge protection, hoarding, frame temporary stability and loading platforms. Design and independent checks per category; permits to load/strike at hold points; no TW altered without TWC approval.
cppText.partial: TW register started; coordinator role to be formalised.
cppText.poor: Temporary works managed informally without register or hold points.

steps.prompt: Work through the temporary works items identified for this project. For each, decide the controls that apply.

items.name: Perimeter access scaffold
items.description: Two-storey independent tied scaffold around the extension, with loading bay and pavement interface.
items.explanation: The loading bay and public interface take this beyond a basic standard configuration — it needs a design, an independent check appropriate to its category, handover before use, and statutory inspections.

items.name: Pad foundation excavations (2.4 m deep)
items.description: Isolated pad excavations for steel bases, plant operating adjacent.
items.explanation: At 2.4 m with plant surcharge nearby, support or safe battering must be designed, inspected at the start of each shift and after events, with entry controlled.

items.name: Mobile crane outrigger mats / working platform
items.description: Platform and mats for the 100 t mobile crane erecting steel.
items.explanation: Crane standing areas need assessed bearing capacity and designed mats/platform, verified before the crane arrives — a hold point before lifting starts.

items.name: Steel frame temporary stability
items.description: Partially-erected frame stability (temporary bracing, bolt completion, erection sequence).
items.explanation: The erection sequence and temporary bracing must come from the designer/fabricator, with hold points before releasing the crane from each stability-critical piece.

items.name: Edge protection to first floor decking
items.description: Proprietary edge protection to leading edges and perimeter of metal decking.
items.explanation: Proprietary systems installed to the manufacturer's instructions are a standard solution, but they still go on the register and get inspected.

items.name: Public boundary hoarding
items.description: 2.4 m timber hoarding along the footpath, gates within.
items.explanation: Hoardings adjacent to the public must resist wind and crowd loads — they need design and periodic inspection, especially after high winds.

items.name: Welfare cabin bases
items.description: Standard level base for single-storey cabins on firm ground.
items.explanation: Simple, low-consequence temporary works can use standard solutions — but they still get registered and checked before use.

items.name: Scaffold loading bay / material hoist base
items.description: Loading platform on the scaffold for palletised materials.
items.explanation: Loading bays carry concentrated loads and change the scaffold's design case — designed, checked, signed off before loading, with safe working load displayed.

steps.learningNote: Everything temporary that holds a load, retains ground, or protects people belongs on the register. The question is never 'register or not' for load-bearing items — it's what design category, what checks, and where the hold points sit.

phases.title: Permits and Inspections
phases.intro: Permits control the highest-risk tasks; inspections prove your controls still work. Choose what this project needs.

steps.prompt: Select the permit systems this project genuinely needs. Over-permitting buries supervisors in paperwork; under-permitting leaves lethal tasks uncontrolled.
steps.explanation: Hot works (welding), breaking ground (buried services), loading temporary works, crane lifts, isolation of the existing building's services at the interface, and leading-edge work all need permit control here. There is no demolition and no confined space work in this scope — adding those permits would be paperwork without purpose.
steps.learningNote: A permit is a formal check that controls are in place immediately before a high-risk task, with a defined start, duration, and sign-back. Use them where a missed control is likely to be fatal — and keep the system small enough to be run properly.

steps.prompt: Set the inspection regime for the project.

options.text: Statutory inspections — scaffold every 7 days and after changes or bad weather, excavations every shift and after events, lifting gear examinations in date — plus weekly and daily checks.
options.feedback: Correct. Statutory inspections are the legal floor; layered daily/weekly checks are how you actually catch deterioration early.

options.text: Each subcontractor inspects its own scaffold, excavations and plant to its own procedures, with copies of the records sent to the site office weekly.
options.feedback: Contractors inspect their own kit, but the PC must monitor the site as a whole — interfaces and shared areas fall between contractors.

options.text: A thorough monthly audit by the company safety advisor, with photos and a scored report, backed by the scaffolder's handover certificate.
options.feedback: Monthly is far outside statutory frequencies for scaffolds and excavations, and conditions change daily — a handover certificate is not an ongoing inspection.
options.consequence: A scaffold tie at the loading bay was removed and went unnoticed until the next monthly audit; the bay was closed and the scaffolder recalled to reinstate it.

options.text: Inspect when conditions change or something looks wrong, so supervisors spend their time where the risk is rather than on routine checks.
options.feedback: Reactive inspection finds defects after they've hurt someone — and statutory inspection frequencies are not optional.
options.criticalFailure: No planned inspection regime
options.consequence: No one inspected the pad excavations after a wet night; the support had shifted and a side collapsed while a groundworker trimmed the base, trapping his legs. RIDDOR-reported.

steps.learningNote: Memorise the statutory rhythm: scaffolds — before use, then every 7 days and after alteration or adverse weather; excavations — start of every shift, and after events affecting stability; lifting equipment — thorough examination certificates current. Inspection findings must be recorded and the written report given to the person it was carried out for within 24 hours; keep reports on site while work continues and retain them afterwards.

cppText.best: Inspection schedule: scaffold before first use, every 7 days and after alteration/adverse weather (recorded); excavations at start of each shift and after rain/events; lifting accessories and plant thorough-examination certificates checked on arrival; weekly recorded site manager inspection; daily supervisor pre-start checks; actions tracked to closure.
cppText.partial: Statutory inspections planned; management inspection layer to be added.

phases.title: High-Risk Activities
phases.intro: Steel, lifting, height and excavations — control the work that can kill in a second.

steps.prompt: Put the steel erection operations into a safe order. The 100 t mobile crane will stand on outrigger mats in the yard, slewing within reach of the occupied office and the public footpath.
steps.context: The crane platform and mats, and the frame's temporary stability, are both on the temporary works register. A permit to load (for the platform) and a lifting permit apply.

activities.label: Appointed Person prepares the lift plan
activities.detail: Crane configuration, outrigger loads, radii, wind limits and slew limits near the office and footpath.

activities.label: Design and check the crane platform and outrigger mats
activities.detail: TW designer works from the AP's outrigger loads and ground data; checked to its design check category.

activities.label: Inspect the built platform; TWC issues permit to load
activities.detail: Hold point: the crane does not set up until the platform is confirmed as built to the design.

activities.label: Set up the exclusion zone and footpath diversion
activities.detail: Barriers under the slew radius, office entrance managed with the client, marshals posted.

activities.label: Rig the crane on the mats and check certificates
activities.detail: Thorough examination reports for crane and accessories; operator, supervisor and slinger cards.

activities.label: Issue the lifting permit and brief the lift team
activities.detail: Crane supervisor briefs signals, wind limits, the erection sequence and stop rules.

activities.label: Land each member, bolt up and fit temporary bracing
activities.detail: Erect in the designer's sequence from MEWPs, with minimum bolts and bracing per the stability design.

activities.label: Release each member from the crane hook
activities.detail: Hold point: the connector confirms bolts and bracing are complete before signalling release.

constraints.reason: The mat and platform design depends on the outrigger loads and crane configuration set in the lift plan.
The built platform can only be inspected and released against an approved, checked design.
Setting the crane up before the platform is verified risks an outrigger punching through and the crane overturning towards the office or footpath.
Rigging, counterweight handling and outrigger set-up are lifting operations in their own right — the public must already be kept clear.
Steel must never be slung over an open footpath or the office entrance; the exclusion zone has to be in place before the first piece is lifted.
The briefing communicates the lift plan — it cannot be given before the plan exists.
The lifting permit depends on the TWC's confirmation that the platform is fit to be loaded.
Thorough examination reports and set-up checks must be confirmed before the crane lifts any steel.
No steel is lifted until the lifting permit is live and the crane team and erectors have been briefed.
Releasing a member before it is bolted and braced leaves the part-built frame unstable — a column or beam can topple towards the office or footpath.

steps.topic: Lifting operations and temporary works — steel erection sequence
steps.learningNote: Near the public the safe order is plan, design and check, verify and permit, segregate, set up, brief, lift — then make each piece stable before the hook lets go. The Appointed Person's lift plan (BS 7121), the TWC's permit to load for the crane platform and the stability hold point before release (BS 5975) are what stop a crane overturning or a part-built frame falling.

steps.prompt: Metal decking installation is next. How should work at height be planned?

options.text: Hierarchy first: ground-level work where possible, nets or airbags under leading edges plus edge protection, MEWPs for access, harnesses only as backup with rescue.
options.feedback: Correct. Collective measures protect everyone without relying on individual behaviour; personal fall arrest is the last resort and demands a rescue plan.

options.text: Issue full-body harnesses and twin-tail lanyards to the whole decking gang, set out tested anchor points on the steel, and brief them to stay clipped on throughout.
options.feedback: Jumping straight to personal protection inverts the hierarchy — collective measures come first, and fall arrest without a rescue plan leaves a fallen worker suspended.

options.text: Let the decking gang use their usual method — they lay deck on frames like this every week and their RAMS was accepted on the last job.
options.feedback: Their 'usual method' is unknown until you've reviewed it against the hierarchy for this building — acceptance on another job is not a review here.
options.consequence: The gang's usual method meant walking the beams to land bundles; a decker slipped at the leading edge and was grabbed by a colleague — a near miss raised at the briefing.

options.text: Ladders and mobile towers for the first-floor deck — it's a single-storey drop and the towers can be moved along beneath the leading edge.
options.feedback: Leading-edge decking work from ladders is not a recognised safe method at any height.
options.consequence: A tower was pushed along with a decker still on it and tipped against the steel; he held on and was unhurt, but decking stopped for a day while access was re-planned.

steps.topic: Work at height — hierarchy of control
steps.learningNote: Avoid work at height where possible; prevent falls with collective measures (platforms, edge protection); mitigate with nets/airbags before harnesses. Any fall-arrest use requires anchor points and a practised rescue plan.

cppText.best: Work at height: collective protection first (edge protection, nets/airbags below leading edges); MEWP access with trained operators and rescue plan; harness use only as last resort against designated anchors; ladders restricted to short-duration access.
cppText.partial: Work at height controls rely primarily on personal fall protection.
cppText.poor: Work at height methods left to individual gangs.

steps.prompt: The 100 t mobile crane arrives Monday for steel erection near the occupied building. What must be in place?

options.text: An Appointed Person's lift plan, in-date thorough examinations for crane and accessories, a crane supervisor and slinger/signaller, verified mats, and an exclusion zone clear of footpath and office.
options.feedback: Correct. Every lifting operation must be planned by a competent appointed person, supervised, and carried out safely — with the public interface designed out of the lift radius.

options.text: Book it as a contract lift so the hire company provides the Appointed Person, lift plan and crew, and confirm the paperwork arrives with the crane.
options.feedback: A genuine contract lift moves duties to the crane contractor, but you must confirm that's what was bought, coordinate the site interface, exclusion zones and ground conditions — those never transfer.

options.text: The CPCS-carded operator has lifted on this business park before; he'll walk the site on arrival, set up and agree the lifting sequence with the erectors.
options.feedback: Lift planning on the morning, by the operator alone, is how cranes end up overturned or overloaded — local experience doesn't replace a lift plan.
options.consequence: Setting up on the morning put an outrigger over a backfilled drainage run; the mat settled during the first lift and the crane was stood down until the ground was checked.

options.text: Start the steel lifts on Monday as booked, with the operator reducing loads or pausing work whenever the cab anemometer shows the wind picking up.
options.feedback: Improvised wind rules are not a lift plan. Wind limits come from the crane and load characteristics, set in advance.
options.criticalFailure: Lifting operations without a lift plan
options.consequence: With no lift plan, a gust swung a beam into the occupied office's window line and broken glass fell onto the footpath. HSE investigated and served a prohibition notice.

steps.learningNote: Lifting operations must be planned by an appointed person, use thoroughly-examined equipment, and be supervised by competent people. Ground bearing, exclusion zones and weather limits are part of the plan, not afterthoughts.

steps.prompt: Before pad foundation excavation starts, the service drawings show 'no known services' in the dig area. What do you do?

options.text: Treat the drawings as a starting point: CAT and Genny scan, hand-dug trial holes at any anomaly, a permit to dig, and a briefing for the driver on located services.
options.feedback: Correct. Utility plans are routinely incomplete or inaccurate. Locate, mark, dig trial holes, and control with a permit.

options.text: Proceed with the excavator using a toothless bucket and a banksman watching every scrape, since the drawings and the client's own survey both show the dig area clear.
options.feedback: Striking an unrecorded cable or main is one of construction's most common serious incidents — drawings alone are never sufficient, and a banksman can't see through soil.
options.criticalFailure: Excavation without service location survey
options.consequence: The bucket struck an unrecorded 11 kV cable; the driver was unhurt but the flash scorched the bucket and cut power to the office. It was reported to HSE as a dangerous occurrence.

options.text: CAT scan the dig area as a check, and bring in a Genny and trial holes only if the CAT picks up a signal or the operator meets anything unusual.
options.feedback: A CAT alone won't find plastic pipes or unenergised cables, and by the time the operator 'feels' a service, it's usually been struck.
options.consequence: The CAT showed nothing, but the bucket split an unrecorded plastic water main; the pad flooded and had to be pumped out and re-trimmed, losing two days.

options.text: Hand-dig every pad excavation to full depth to be completely safe, accepting that it doubles the groundworks duration.
options.feedback: Hand-digging everywhere is disproportionate when scanning and trial holes can target the risk — safe digging practice near located services is the balanced answer.

steps.learningNote: The sequence is: obtain plans, scan and mark, permit to dig, trial holes to confirm, safe digging practice near services, and treat every unidentified anomaly as live until proven otherwise.

phases.title: Environmental Management
phases.intro: The environment doesn't get a second chance either — control waste, water, dust and noise before they leave the site.

steps.prompt: Set the site's environmental controls.

options.text: Segregated waste with licensed carriers and transfer notes, bunded fuel with spill kits, drain protection, dust suppression, agreed working hours and regular updates for the neighbouring tenants.
options.feedback: Correct. Waste duty of care, pollution prevention and nuisance control are all legal duties — and neighbour goodwill protects your programme.

options.text: One mixed-waste container on site, with a licensed carrier who segregates at the transfer station and the waste transfer notes filed in the site office.
options.feedback: Legal if the carrier is licensed and documented, but wasteful and costly — and it does nothing for dust, water or noise.

options.text: Introduce the full environmental controls at envelope stage, when cutting, packaging and sealants arrive; groundworks mainly generate inert spoil.
options.feedback: Groundworks is the highest-pollution-risk stage: silt, fuel and spoil. Controls are needed first, not last.
options.consequence: Silty water pumped from the pad excavations ran into the surface water drain and discoloured the brook downstream; the Environment Agency issued a warning letter.

options.text: Wash out the concrete wagons at the yard gully, which runs to the foul sewer on the old site drawings, rather than setting up a lined bay.
options.feedback: Concrete washout is highly alkaline and toxic to watercourses. Old drawings don't prove where a gully discharges — this one feeds surface water, and the discharge is a pollution offence.
options.criticalFailure: Concrete washout discharged to surface water drain
options.consequence: The gully discharged to surface water, not foul; washout killed fish in the brook downstream and the Environment Agency prosecuted the company for a pollution offence.

steps.topic: Environmental controls — waste, water, dust, noise
steps.learningNote: Know where every drain leads. Bund fuels, protect drains, contain concrete washout, damp down dust, segregate waste with duty-of-care paperwork, and manage noise hours and neighbour relations proactively.

cppText.best: Environmental controls: segregated waste streams, licensed carriers, waste transfer notes retained; bunded fuel storage with spill kits and trained personnel; surface water drain protected; designated concrete washout; dust damping; deliveries and noisy works within agreed hours; neighbour notification and complaints log.
cppText.partial: Basic waste and fuel controls; dust/noise/neighbour arrangements to be developed.
cppText.poor: Environmental controls deferred to later project stages.

steps.prompt: Cutting and grinding operations will create dust. Occupational health controls?

options.text: Cut less by ordering and design, then on-tool extraction or water suppression, face-fit-tested RPE as backup, task rotation and health surveillance where needed.
options.feedback: Correct. Silica dust, noise and vibration cause far more ill-health than accidents cause injury — control at source first, protect the person second, monitor health where required.

options.text: Issue FFP3 disposable masks to everyone working in or passing through the cutting area, and make wearing them a site rule enforced by the supervisors on their daily rounds.
options.feedback: RPE without source control, face-fit testing and clean-shaven policy delivers a fraction of its rated protection.

options.text: Treat dust as low risk here: cutting is limited to short, occasional tasks outdoors, where the wind disperses it quickly.
options.feedback: There is no safe level of respirable crystalline silica. Short tasks still add to cumulative disease, and the wind carries the dust to others nearby.
options.consequence: Dry block cutting beside the office's air intake drew dust into the building; tenants complained of dust on desks and the client halted all cutting for two days.

options.text: Schedule all cutting for 7am, before the other trades arrive, so the fewest people are exposed and the dust has settled by mid-morning.
options.feedback: This concentrates unprotected exposure on the cutters and creates a noise nuisance — it controls nothing at source.
options.consequence: Cutting started before the agreed hours; tenants complained about the noise and the council's environmental health officer visited the site.

steps.learningNote: Health hazards follow the same hierarchy as safety: eliminate, reduce at source (on-tool extraction, water), then protect the person (fitted RPE, hearing protection) and monitor (exposure and health surveillance).

phases.title: Incident / Challenge Events
phases.intro: Sites never run to plan. Deal with what the project throws at you — your judgement under pressure is what's being tested.

steps.prompt: EVENT: A member of the public with a pushchair is found inside the site boundary, using your access gate as a shortcut while the gate was propped open for deliveries.

options.text: Escort them out, stop deliveries until the gate is controlled, find out how it happened, fix the gate control (discipline, marshal) and brief the workforce.
options.feedback: Correct. Treat unauthorised access as a near miss: make safe, then fix the system failure that allowed it — not just this instance.

options.text: Escort them out, apologise, and remind the gate operative that the gate must be shut between vehicles from now on.
options.feedback: You removed the person but not the cause. A reminder is not a corrective action — the gate needs positive control, such as a marshal, while deliveries run.

options.text: Escort them out and add 'No unauthorised access — construction site' signs facing the footpath on both sides of the gate.
options.feedback: The person walked past existing signs. Physical control failed; signage won't fix it.
options.consequence: The gate stayed propped for deliveries; the next day a dog walker cut through the site and was nearly struck by a reversing telehandler.

options.text: Escort them out and carry on — the gate is only open while deliveries are running, this was a one-off, and nobody came anywhere near the open excavations or plant.
options.feedback: Children follow the same route the pushchair did. Unauthorised access next to excavations and lifting is a fatality pathway.
options.criticalFailure: Ignored unauthorised public access onto site
options.consequence: The gate stayed propped; a child followed the same shortcut after school and was found beside an open pad excavation. The police were called and HSE served an improvement notice.

steps.learningNote: Near misses are free lessons. Investigate the system failure (why was the gate open and unattended?), correct it, and share the learning — the same event with a child ends differently.

steps.prompt: EVENT: During Friday's pour, the concrete pump blocks and the delivery backs up. The groundworks foreman proposes washing out the part-used wagon behind the skips 'where it won't be in the way' — three metres from the surface water drain.

options.text: Stop him. Direct washout to the designated lined washout area, protect the drain, and deal with the delay through the concrete supplier.
options.feedback: Correct. A washout near a surface water drain is a pollution incident waiting one rain shower. The designated facility exists exactly for this.

options.text: Allow it where he suggests, but have him lay heavy-gauge polythene inside a sandbag bund first so the washwater can't run towards the drain.
options.feedback: A polythene sheet and sandbags three metres from a drain is token protection — alkaline water overtops low bunds and runs off sheets.
options.consequence: Rain overtopped the sandbag bund overnight; grey washwater reached the surface water drain, the client's facilities team reported it, and cleaning the gully cost a day.

options.text: Allow it this once given the pour is at risk, and record the reason in the site diary so there is a clear audit trail.
options.feedback: Documenting a pollution risk you allowed makes it worse, not better. Pollution offences carry serious penalties.
options.criticalFailure: Permitted concrete washout near surface water drain
options.consequence: Washwater ran straight into the surface water drain and turned the brook downstream grey. The Environment Agency attended and the diary entry became evidence.

options.text: Send the part-used wagon back to the plant full and accept the cost of the wasted load to protect the drain.
options.feedback: Environmentally safe, but the designated washout was the planned, cheaper answer. Know your own site facilities.

steps.learningNote: Pollution prevention is mostly about pathways: know your drains, keep washout/fuel/silt away from them, and never trade a permanent environmental harm for an hour of programme.

phases.title: Progress Review
phases.intro: Mid-project: the client reviews progress, and how you communicate and supervise now determines how the second half runs.

steps.prompt: At the progress meeting the client asks you to recover a two-week slippage by working the steel and decking gangs 7 days a week and overlapping trades on the frame. Your response?

options.text: Re-plan the recovery: find what can genuinely compress (procurement, sequencing, extra supervised resource), assess fatigue and interface risks, and offer the client a plan you can supervise safely.
options.feedback: Correct. Real programme recovery comes from re-planning, not exhaustion. Overlapping trades under a live frame multiplies interface risk unless it's engineered.

options.text: Agree 7-day weeks for the steel and decking gangs for the next fortnight — they've asked for the overtime and the weather window is good.
options.feedback: Fatigue degrades exactly the vigilance that steel erection and lifting depend on. Willing workers don't make it safe.
options.consequence: By the second weekend a tired slinger mis-hooked a bundle of decking; it slipped from the sling onto the deck below, clear of anyone. The near miss was reported.

options.text: Decline in writing: the slippage came from the client's late design changes, so any recovery is a variation at the client's cost and risk.
options.feedback: Programme is your problem too. Refusing to engage — even with a fair point about cause — costs the relationship and misses genuinely safe recovery options.
