options.consequence: The client escalated to your director, who agreed a recovery without site input; cladders were programmed under live steel erection and a dropped bolt narrowly missed one.

options.text: Strike the safety nets ahead of the decking to speed the cycle, with the gang clipped to the steel on harnesses for the remaining edges.
options.feedback: Removing collective protection to buy programme is exactly the trade the law and your own plan forbid.
options.criticalFailure: Removed collective fall protection under programme pressure
options.consequence: With the nets struck, a decker unclipped to move a bundle and fell through an open bay to the ground floor, fracturing his pelvis. HSE served a prohibition notice.

steps.topic: Programme pressure and safe recovery planning
steps.learningNote: When pressed on programme: re-sequence, resource and supervise — never de-control. A recovery plan that degrades controls isn't recovery; it's borrowing against an accident.

steps.prompt: Your weekly inspection finds housekeeping slipping: trip hazards on the decking, cable runs across walkways, and the fire point partially blocked by plasterboard. What's the effective response?

options.text: Clear the fire point now, give supervisors named actions and deadlines, raise it at the daily briefing, and track it at subcontractor meetings until it holds.
options.feedback: Correct. Fix the immediate danger, then assign ownership and follow up through your management routines — standards are set by what you walk past.

options.text: Issue an all-site email and a housekeeping toolbox talk sheet, copied to every subcontractor's contracts manager for action.
options.feedback: Emails and handouts don't move plasterboard. Named actions and follow-up do — and the fire point is blocked right now.
options.consequence: At the next fire drill the extinguishers couldn't be reached past the plasterboard, and the client's insurer recorded it as a site defect requiring a response.

options.text: Hire two labourers to clear up behind all trades for the rest of the job, and contra-charge the cost across the subcontract accounts.
options.feedback: It helps, but it also teaches the trades that mess is someone else's job — pair it with accountability.

options.text: Record the findings in the monthly report and raise them with each trade at the next subcontractor progress meeting, since none of it has actually stopped work yet.
options.feedback: A blocked fire point is not cosmetic. Slips and trips are the biggest cause of injury, and blocked escape kills in fires.
options.criticalFailure: Blocked fire point left unaddressed
options.consequence: A cable across the decking walkway tripped a fitter carrying a sheet; he fell against the edge protection and broke his wrist — a RIDDOR specified injury.

steps.learningNote: Inspection without enforcement teaches people the standards are optional. Escalate through supervision: brief, assign, verify, and make persistent failure a commercial conversation with the subcontractor.

steps.prompt: How do you keep the workforce engaged in safety through the project's second half?

options.text: Consult, don't broadcast: short talks on current work, visible action on concerns and near misses, gangs involved in method reviews, and feedback on what changed.
options.feedback: Correct. Consultation is a legal duty and your best sensor network — people report what they see acted on.

options.text: A monthly all-site safety briefing in the canteen covering every current topic in one session, with signed attendance sheets and a short quiz to test understanding.
options.feedback: One long generic session is retention-free. Short, current, task-linked talks work.
options.consequence: The monthly briefing came before envelope work started; when a MEWP basket stuck, the fitters didn't know the rescue arrangements and the response was slow.

options.text: A monthly bonus for each gang that records zero incidents and zero near misses, so every operative has a direct financial stake in working safely on the job.
options.feedback: Rewarding zero reports suppresses reporting, not incidents. You lose your early warnings.
options.consequence: Near-miss reports dried up; a gang kept quiet about a dropped scaffold tube that landed near the footpath until a tenant reported it to the client.

options.text: Take a firm line: anyone seen breaking a site rule is removed from site, so the workforce knows standards are non-negotiable.
options.feedback: Fear stops reporting and honest conversation. Fair, consistent responses distinguish violations from system failures.
options.consequence: Operatives stopped reporting problems for fear of removal; a known MEWP fault went unreported until the basket stuck at height with two fitters in it.

steps.learningNote: Consult the workforce in good time on matters affecting their health and safety. Near-miss reporting rises when people see action; it dies when reports vanish or trigger blame.

phases.title: Handover
phases.intro: Finish safely and hand over cleanly — the project isn't done until the building and its information are in the client's hands.

steps.prompt: Practical completion is two weeks away. What does a proper handover require from you?

options.text: Give the principal designer the H&S file information (as-builts, residual risks, maintenance access, materials), complete commissioning and O&Ms, close out snags, and plan a safe demobilisation.
options.feedback: Correct. The health and safety file protects everyone who maintains, cleans, refurbishes or demolishes this building for decades — it's a legal deliverable, not a courtesy.

options.text: Hand over the keys at practical completion and issue the O&Ms and as-builts as subcontractors finish assembling them over the following months.
options.feedback: Information assembled after the team disperses is incomplete information. Collect it progressively; deliver it at handover.
options.consequence: The roof access and anchor details never reached the file; the client's first maintenance contractor found no test records and couldn't safely reach the roof plant.

options.text: The H&S file is compiled by the principal designer, so your role is to forward any subcontractor documents they specifically request.
options.feedback: The PD compiles the file, but the principal contractor must provide the information — the file is only as good as what you feed it.
options.consequence: The principal designer received no residual-risk information on the steel connections or decking; the file was returned incomplete and retention was withheld.

options.text: Focus the final fortnight on the finishes the client will inspect, with documentation completed by the site administrator once snagging closes.
options.feedback: Cosmetics over content: the residual-risk information is what prevents the next contractor's accident.
options.consequence: The O&M and as-built information was still missing at handover; the client declined to accept the building and practical completion slipped by a week.

steps.topic: Handover — health and safety file and close-out
steps.learningNote: Plan handover from day one: collect as-builts, certificates, residual risk information and maintenance requirements progressively. Demobilisation (scaffold strike, hoarding removal, reinstatement) is itself a phase needing RAMS and TW control.

cppText.best: Handover: H&S file information provided to Principal Designer (as-builts, residual risks, safe maintenance/access, hazardous materials used); O&M manuals and commissioning certificates complete; snagging closed; demobilisation planned with TW control for scaffold strike and hoarding removal; client familiarisation completed.
cppText.partial: Handover documentation partially assembled at completion.
cppText.poor: Handover information left to follow after completion.
cppText.unsafe: No structured handover of safety information.

phases.title: Final Score and Feedback
phases.intro: Project complete. Review your performance across every discipline.

steps.title: Project handed over
body: The extension is complete and the client has taken occupation.

Your decisions through 22 weeks of planning, set-up, high-risk work and handover have been assessed across legal compliance, safety control, planning, temporary works, environment, programme and quality.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: The excavator bucket snags an unmarked plastic duct in a pad excavation. Nothing visible is damaged, but the duct isn't on any drawing.

options.text: Stop the dig, treat the duct as live, clear and cordon the excavation, and get it identified with the utility owners and a scan before work resumes there.
options.feedback: Correct. Unknown services are treated as live until positively identified. A 'plastic duct' can carry HV cables.

options.text: Hand-dig carefully around the duct to expose it and see what it carries, then decide whether the excavation can continue around it.
options.feedback: Hand exposure of an unidentified duct without isolation confirmation still risks cable strike through the duct wall.
options.consequence: Hand exposure split the duct and revealed a live LV cable; the spade stopped short of the insulation. The near miss was reported to the network operator.

options.text: Log the duct, mark it with a stake and keep digging half a metre clear of it — it's undamaged plastic, it isn't on any service drawing and the CAT scan was clear.
options.feedback: Unidentified means uncontrolled. The next bucket may find the same duct where it isn't visible.
options.criticalFailure: Continued excavation after striking unknown service
options.consequence: The duct carried a live 11 kV cable that turned under the next pad; the bucket struck it there, the flash damaged the excavator and the strike was reported to HSE.

options.text: Move that gang to another pad excavation for today and decide about the duct tomorrow when the site engineer is back.
options.feedback: Relocating work is fine, but the discovery still needs immediate reporting, cordoning and identification — other excavations may hold the same unknown run.

eventPool.learningNote: On striking or finding any unknown service: stop, keep people clear, treat as live, and get positive identification before resuming. Report it so the whole site learns the drawings are incomplete.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: Overnight storms have half-filled the deepest pad excavation with water. The sides show slumping at one corner. Concrete is booked for 10am.

options.text: Prohibit entry, re-inspect the excavation and its support before any decision, pump out only once stability is confirmed, and rebook the pour if needed.
options.feedback: Correct. Excavations must be inspected after any event likely to affect stability — rain and slumping are exactly that. The pour waits for the ground.

options.text: Pump it out fast and keep the 10am pour: the slumped corner sits outside the pad footprint, and the concrete will consolidate the base once it's placed.
options.feedback: Sending anyone into a slumping, waterlogged excavation to prep and pour is a burial risk. Concrete does not fix unstable sides.
options.criticalFailure: Workers exposed to unstable excavation after weather event
options.consequence: The slumped corner collapsed while a groundworker positioned the pump hose; he was buried to the waist and rescued with leg injuries. It was reported under RIDDOR.

options.text: Pump out and pour on time, with the gang working from the edges only and the pump hose fed in from the stable side, well away from the slumped corner.
options.feedback: Edge loading on slumping sides makes collapse more likely, and 'stay out of the hole' rarely survives contact with a stuck pump line.
options.consequence: The edge gave way under the pump hose operator's feet; he stepped back in time, but the side slumped into the base and the pour was abandoned.

options.text: Cancel today's pour and stop all excavation work on site for 48 hours as a blanket precaution until the ground dries out.
options.feedback: Safe but unmeasured — a competent post-event inspection could return stable excavations to work sooner.

eventPool.learningNote: Inspect excavations at the start of every shift and after anything that could affect stability: rain, frost, adjacent loads, or strikes. The inspection decides when work resumes — not the concrete booking.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A telehandler arrives on hire. The driver has no thorough examination certificate for it and says 'it's all on the hire company's system'.

options.text: Quarantine the telehandler until its current thorough examination report and daily check records are produced, and check the operator's card while you wait.
options.feedback: Correct. Lifting equipment needs a current thorough examination — no certificate, no use. Arrival is also the moment to verify the operator, not after an incident.

options.text: Let it work on light duties today and ask the hire desk to email the thorough examination report before it lifts anything heavy.
options.feedback: If the examination has lapsed, today is exactly when the defect it would have found gets someone hurt.
options.consequence: The examination had lapsed; on 'light duties' a worn carriage chain slipped while lifting a pallet of blocks and the load dropped short of the scaffold. No one was hurt.

options.text: Do a walk-round check with the driver — tyres, hydraulics, forks, chains, load indicator — and put it to work if everything looks sound and the daily check is signed.
options.feedback: A visual walk-around cannot substitute for a thorough examination of lifting-critical components.
options.consequence: The walk-round missed a cracked fork heel; it failed while lifting decking bundles and the load fell inside the exclusion zone. The hire company investigated.

options.text: Reject the machine at the gate, terminate the hire contract and source a replacement from a different supplier.
options.feedback: You've removed the risk, but a phone call usually produces the certificate within the hour — quarantine first, escalate if it doesn't appear.

eventPool.topic: Plant and lifting equipment — thorough examination
eventPool.learningNote: Check on arrival, every time: thorough examination certificate, daily/weekly check records, and operator competence. Make it a documented site rule so the gate stops what paperwork doesn't.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: An experienced groundworker refuses to wear safety glasses while breaking out concrete, saying they fog up and 'he's done this for 20 years'.

options.text: Stop the task, deal with the fogging by supplying anti-fog or alternative eyewear, make clear the task doesn't run without eye protection, and check the fix works.
options.feedback: Correct. Most PPE refusal is a usability problem wearing a defiance mask. Fix the kit, hold the standard.

options.text: Remove him from site and start the disciplinary process today, so the rest of the gang sees the eye protection rule is enforced.
options.feedback: Escalation without investigation loses the workforce and doesn't fix the fogging that the next worker will also face.
options.consequence: The gang closed ranks and the fogging problem was never fixed; another breaker took his glasses off to see and was treated for a concrete chip in his eye.

options.text: Let him carry on without them — he's experienced, he has signed a disclaimer accepting the risk, the breaking out is nearly finished and the rest of the gang wear theirs.
options.feedback: Disclaimers have no legal effect on your duty. Flying concrete fragments don't respect experience.
options.criticalFailure: Allowed high-risk task without required PPE
options.consequence: A concrete fragment struck his unprotected eye and he lost part of his sight. It was reported under RIDDOR and HSE investigated the site's PPE enforcement.

options.text: Move him to a different task for the rest of the day and give the breaking out to another member of the gang.
options.feedback: You've protected him but dodged the standard — the fogging problem and the precedent both remain.

eventPool.learningNote: PPE is the last line of defence but it's still mandatory where assessed. Investigate refusals — comfort and fit issues are fixable — and apply the standard consistently to everyone, including visitors and managers.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: You find that two scaffold ties have been removed at first-floor level to let the cladders install panels, without any approval. The scaffold is still in use.

options.text: Clear and close the affected scaffold now, have the scaffold contractor reinstate or redesign the ties, require a recorded inspection before reuse, and investigate the failure with the cladders.
options.feedback: Correct. Ties are structural. Unauthorised alteration voids the handover — the scaffold is unproven until reinspected.

options.text: Have the cladders refit both ties exactly where they found them using the original fittings, and check them yourself before work restarts.
options.feedback: Cladders are not scaffolders, and a site manager's look is not a scaffold inspection. Structural reinstatement by the wrong trade compounds the failure.
options.criticalFailure: Unauthorised scaffold alteration handled without competent reinstatement
options.consequence: The cladders refitted the ties to the wrong members; a lift partially collapsed when loaded with panels and was reported under RIDDOR as a dangerous occurrence.

options.text: Log it for the scaffold contractor's weekly inspection on Friday and tell the cladders to keep heavy panels off that lift until then.
options.feedback: Days more use of a compromised scaffold means days of collapse exposure — keeping panels off one lift doesn't restore the ties.
options.consequence: Before Friday, a gusty afternoon flexed the untied section and boards shifted; the cladders came down on their own and reported the near miss.

options.text: Remove the cladding contractor's gang from site permanently, and write to all trades making clear that any unauthorised alteration means removal.
options.feedback: Accountability matters, but the immediate structural risk and the systemic fix (how do trades request adaptations?) matter more.

eventPool.learningNote: No one alters temporary works except the competent contractor under TWC control. Give trades a fast legitimate route to request adaptations — if the official route takes a week, people will keep making their own.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: Breaking through the existing wall for the link corridor, a joiner finds old insulation board debris behind the plasterboard that isn't mentioned in the refurbishment and demolition asbestos survey.

options.text: Stop work in the area, seal and sign it, decontaminate as a precaution, and have it sampled by an accredited surveyor before anything is disturbed further.
options.feedback: Correct. Suspect it, stop, seal, sample. Insulation board is a licensed-work material if confirmed — disturbance without controls exposes everyone nearby.

options.text: Double-bag the debris, damp the area down and carry on — the refurbishment and demolition survey covered this wall, sampled it and found no asbestos at all.
options.feedback: The find proves the survey wrong for this location. Continuing spreads fibres through the occupied building's shared spaces.
options.criticalFailure: Continued work after discovering suspect asbestos material
options.consequence: The board was confirmed as asbestos insulation board; three operatives were exposed and debris reached the office corridor, which was closed for decontamination. HSE investigated.

options.text: Stop the joiner, have him photograph the board and email it to the asbestos surveyor, and restart once the surveyor gives an opinion.
options.feedback: Asbestos cannot be identified from photographs. The area stays live-risk while emails circulate.
options.consequence: The surveyor would not identify it from a photo; the opening stayed unsealed for two days with trades passing until samples were taken and the area cleaned.

options.text: Stop that task and tape off the wall, but let the electricians and decorators carry on elsewhere in the same room to save the day.
options.feedback: Fibre release doesn't respect task boundaries — the exclusion applies to the area, not the task.
options.consequence: Samples confirmed asbestos insulation board; the electricians and decorators in the room needed decontamination and the room's finishes were stripped and redone.

eventPool.learningNote: Surveys have limits — voids and concealed areas surprise everyone. The drill is always: stop, prevent access, don't disturb further, sample and assess by competent people, and review the survey's reliability elsewhere.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A joiner falls from a stepladder and fractures his wrist. He's taken to hospital and will be off work for several weeks. The subcontractor's supervisor suggests recording it as a minor first-aid case 'to keep the stats clean'.

options.text: Make sure he's cared for, preserve the scene, investigate the fall, and report the specified injury under RIDDOR — then act on what the investigation finds.
options.feedback: Correct. A fracture (other than fingers/thumbs/toes) is a specified injury and must be reported. The investigation matters more than the statistic.

options.text: Log it as a first-aid case for now, and report under RIDDOR only if he is still off work when the over-seven-day threshold is reached.
options.feedback: Unsafe. A wrist fracture is a specified injury, reportable without delay whatever the absence. Misrecording it is an offence in itself, separate from the accident.
options.criticalFailure: Failed to report a RIDDOR specified injury
options.consequence: HSE learned of the fracture from the joiner's own account; the late, misrecorded report led to an investigation and an improvement notice on accident reporting.

options.text: Leave the RIDDOR report to the subcontractor as his employer, and ask for a copy of the report and its investigation for the site file.
options.feedback: The reporting duty sits with the injured person's employer, but as PC you must ensure it happens, investigate the site causes, and act on them.

options.text: Record it in the site accident book and run a stepladder toolbox talk for all trades next week, so the lessons are acted on quickly rather than lost in paperwork.
options.feedback: Training without reporting hides the event from the system designed to prevent the next one — and it's non-compliant.
options.consequence: The unreported fracture surfaced at an HSE visit and a fee for intervention followed; the stepladder's split stile, the real cause, had never been found.

eventPool.learningNote: Know the reportable categories: deaths, specified injuries, over-7-day incapacitation, occupational diseases, dangerous occurrences and certain gas events. Reporting is the employer's duty; the PC ensures it happens and leads the site learning.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: A MEWP with two envelope fitters develops a hydraulic fault and is stuck at 9 metres. The ground controls won't respond. One fitter suggests climbing down the boom.

options.text: Forbid climbing down, keep them calm and clipped in, run the rescue plan — emergency lowering by a trained person or the second MEWP — then quarantine the machine.
options.feedback: Correct. This is why the rescue plan exists. Climbing a boom has killed people the fault never would have.

options.text: Call the fire service and wait with the fitters — they have the aerial equipment and trained crews for exactly this kind of rescue.
options.feedback: The fire service is a backstop, not a plan — response times leave people stranded and pressure builds to self-rescue. Your own rescue arrangements come first.

options.text: Let the more experienced fitter climb down the boom, clipped on with his lanyard as he goes, while the other stays in the basket and keeps the fire service updated.
options.feedback: Boom climbing at 9 m, even clipped on, is a fall from height waiting to happen — and he has left his colleague alone.
options.criticalFailure: Permitted boom climb-down instead of rescue plan
options.consequence: The fitter lost his footing on the boom and fell onto the scaffold below, fracturing his ankle. HSE investigated the attempted self-rescue.

options.text: Have the telehandler raise a pallet cage alongside the basket so the fitters can step across and be lowered to the ground.
options.feedback: An improvised, non-integrated platform transfer at height replaces one emergency with a worse one.
options.consequence: The cage swayed as the first fitter stepped across and he grabbed the guardrail; both came down shaken and the hire company withdrew the telehandler.

eventPool.learningNote: Every MEWP operation needs a rescue plan before work starts: trained people on the ground familiar with auxiliary/emergency lowering, and a means of rescue that doesn't rely on the stranded machine. Practise it.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: On Monday morning the police tell you teenagers were seen climbing the hoarding on Saturday night. You find a trainer print halfway up the scaffold and an access ladder left in place over the weekend.

options.text: Treat it as a serious near miss: inspect the scaffold for interference before use, remove or board ladder access out of hours, improve lighting and security, immobilise plant, and brief the findings.
options.feedback: Correct. The site owes duties even to people who enter without permission — and the law expressly expects you to anticipate that children and young people are inquisitive and may trespass. The scaffold is also unproven until inspected after possible interference.

options.text: Remove the ladder access out of hours from tonight, lock the ladders in the container and carry on as normal — that was the route they used to get up.
options.feedback: Removing out-of-hours ladder access is a key control, but you've skipped the post-interference scaffold inspection and the wider security review — plant, materials and excavations are still reachable.

options.text: Add 'Danger — keep out, trespassers will be prosecuted' signs along the hoarding and ask the police to add the site to their patrols.
options.feedback: Signs and patrols do not discharge the duty. Physical security, not warnings, protects children who ignore signs — and the scaffold still needs inspecting after possible interference.
options.consequence: The teenagers returned and climbed the scaffold again; one slipped between lifts and broke his wrist, and his parents brought a claim against the company.

options.text: Log the police call and the trainer print and carry on as normal — trespassers enter at their own risk and the hoarding is full height.
options.feedback: This is the classic misconception. Occupiers owe duties to unauthorised entrants too, and courts expect extra precautions where child trespass is foreseeable — which it now demonstrably is.
options.criticalFailure: Ignored foreseeable child trespass risk after a known incursion
options.consequence: Teenagers got in again and one fell through an unboarded gap in the scaffold to the ground, suffering serious injuries. HSE and the police investigated site security.

eventPool.topic: Occupiers' liability and site security out of hours
eventPool.learningNote: Duties to people on your site do not stop at lawful visitors — they extend to trespassers, and expressly to children, who must be anticipated to be inquisitive. Secure the obvious attractions: remove or board scaffold access, immobilise plant, lock away substances, light the boundary, and inspect anything that may have been interfered with before it is used again.

eventPool.prompt: EVENT: You find blockwork being laid from a 1.8 m high working platform with no guardrails. The gang foreman waves you off: 'Work at height rules only kick in above two metres — this is under, so we're fine.'

options.text: Stop the work: there's no two-metre threshold — any fall liable to cause injury counts. Fit guardrails and toe boards before reuse and correct the misconception.
options.feedback: Correct. The two-metre rule disappeared with the Work at Height Regulations — the duty applies wherever a fall could cause injury, and a 1.8 m fall onto blocks can easily be fatal. Platforms need proper edge protection: top rail, no large unprotected gaps, and a toe board.

options.text: Let them finish the current lift while the scaffolder brings guardrails and toe boards, and stop the gang if they aren't fitted by lunchtime.
options.feedback: The exposure is now, not at lunchtime. Tolerating an unguarded platform 'for a few hours' is how falls happen — and it tells the gang the standard is negotiable.
options.consequence: The guardrails didn't arrive before lunch and the gang worked on; a bricklayer stepped back off the platform onto the blocks below and badly sprained his ankle.

options.text: Issue harnesses to the gang so they can carry on while guardrails are sourced, with anchor slings round the nearest steel column.
options.feedback: Personal fall protection is below collective protection in the hierarchy — and on a low platform with no designed anchors, harnesses are largely theatre. Guardrails are the right control; work waits for them.

options.text: Accept the foreman's point: the platform is under two metres, the gang are experienced bricklayers, and a low working platform is lower risk than going up the scaffold.
options.feedback: The two-metre threshold is a myth. Low falls kill and maim regularly — the law asks whether a fall is liable to cause injury, not how far it is.
options.criticalFailure: Permitted unguarded working platform based on the 'two-metre rule' myth
options.consequence: A bricklayer stepped back off the unguarded platform and fell 1.8 m onto stacked blocks, suffering a serious head injury. HSE served a prohibition notice.

eventPool.topic: Work at height — definition and edge protection standards
eventPool.learningNote: Work at height is any work where a person could fall a distance liable to cause personal injury — there is no minimum height threshold. Follow the hierarchy: avoid, then prevent falls collectively (guardrails around 950 mm with no gap over 470 mm, plus toe boards), then personal prevention, then mitigation — with personal fall-arrest as the last resort, never the first fix.

modelAnswerNotes: Pre-construction information obtained and reviewed before planning; CPP in place, proportionate and live before mobilisation.
Duty holders appointed in writing; F10 notified and displayed; competence verified for all high-risk trades.

Site set-up: hoarding on the public boundary with separate vehicle/pedestrian gates; welfare cluster near the entrance; segregated routes; fuel bunded away from the drain with spill kit and drain protection; crane and exclusion zones clear of the footpath and occupied building.
Welfare compliant from day one; induction before entry; signing in/out as emergency roll-call.
Principal risks: work at height, lifting, vehicle interface, excavation, frame stability — each with specific RAMS, reviewed and briefed.

TWC appointed; 8 temporary works items on the register with correct design categories, checks and hold points (permit to load scaffold loading bay, crane platform verification, frame stability sequence).
Permits: hot works, dig, load, lifting, isolation, roof access — no more, no fewer.
Statutory inspection rhythm: scaffold 7-day/after events, excavations each shift, thorough examinations checked at the gate.
Environment: segregated waste with duty-of-care notes, protected drain, designated washout, dust suppression at source, agreed hours and neighbour liaison.
Events handled by stop–make safe–investigate–fix the system, never by normalising the deviation.
Handover: H&S file information delivered progressively, O&Ms complete, demobilisation planned under TW control.
